paragraphs: The Baroness de Stael speaks the same language as the lady I have just quoted, only with more enthusiasm. Her eulogy of Rousseau happened to fall into my hands, and her sentiments — which are shared by too many of my sex — may serve as the text for a few comments. “Though Rousseau,” she observes, “has endeavoured to prevent women from interfering in public affairs, and acting a brilliant part in the theatre of politics; yet, in speaking of them, how much has he done it to their satisfaction! If he wished to deprive them of some rights, foreign to their sex, how has he for ever restored to them all those to which it has a claim! And in attempting to diminish their influence over the deliberations of men, how sacredly has he established the empire they have over their happiness! In aiding them to descend from an usurped throne, he has firmly seated them upon that to which they were destined by nature; and though he be full of indignation against them when they endeavour to resemble men, yet when they come before him with all THE CHARMS WEAKNESSES, VIRTUES, and ERRORS, OF their sex, his respect for their PERSONS amounts almost to adoration.” Quite true! — for no sensualist ever worshipped more fervently at the shrine of beauty. His reverence for the person was so devout, in fact, that apart from the virtue of chastity, for obvious reasons, he wanted to see it decorated with nothing but charms, weaknesses and errors. He feared that the severity of reason might upset the soft playfulness of love. The master wanted a meretricious slave to caress, wholly dependent on his reason and his generosity; he had no wish for a companion whom he would be obliged to esteem, or for a friend to whom he could entrust his children’s education should death take their father from them before he had completed that sacred task. He denies woman reason, bars her from knowledge and steers her away from truth; yet he is forgiven, because “he admits the passion of love.” It would take some ingenuity to explain why women should feel so indebted to him for admitting love on these terms, when he plainly admits it only to give men relaxation and to continue the species; but he spoke with passion, and that powerful spell worked on the sensibility of a young admirer. “What signifies it,” this rhapsodist goes on, “to women, that his reason disputes with them the empire, when his heart is devotedly theirs.” What women ought to contend for is not empire but equality. Yet even if all they wanted was to prolong their reign, they should not rely wholly on their persons; for although beauty may win a heart, it cannot hold it — not even while the beauty is in full bloom — unless the mind contributes at least some graces.

Once women are enlightened enough to see where their real interest lies, on a grand scale, I am convinced they will readily give up every prerogative of love that is not mutual (speaking of these as lasting prerogatives) in return for the calm satisfaction of friendship and the tender trust that comes from habitual esteem. They will neither put on insolent airs before marriage nor grovel in submission afterwards; instead, trying to behave as reasonable creatures in both situations, they will avoid being tumbled from a throne onto a stool.

Madame Genlis has written several entertaining books for children, and her letters on education contain many useful suggestions which sensible parents will certainly make use of; but her outlook is narrow, and her prejudices are as unreasonable as they are strong.

I shall pass over her vehement argument that punishment in the next life is eternal, since I blush to think that any human being should argue vehemently for such a cause; I shall merely make a few remarks on the absurd way she lets parental authority take the place of reason. For everywhere she preaches not only BLIND submission to parents, but submission to the opinion of the world as well.*

(*Footnote. A person is not to act in this or that way, even when convinced that doing so is right, because some ambiguous circumstances might lead the world to SUSPECT different motives. This is sacrificing the substance for the shadow. If people will simply watch their own hearts and act rightly as far as they are able to judge, they can wait patiently for the world’s opinion to come round. It is best to be guided by a single motive — for justice has too often been sacrificed to propriety — which is just another word for convenience.)

She tells the story of a young man who, at his father’s express wish, becomes engaged to a girl with a fortune. Before the wedding can take place the girl loses her fortune and is cast friendless upon the world. The father resorts to the most infamous tricks to part his son from her; and when the son uncovers his villainy and, obeying the call of honour, marries the girl, nothing follows but misery — because, if you please, he married WITHOUT his father’s consent. What ground is left for religion or morality to stand on, when justice is flouted like this? In the same spirit she portrays an accomplished young woman as willing to marry anyone her MAMMA saw fit to recommend, and as actually marrying the young man of her own choice without any stirrings of passion, since a well-educated girl had no time to fall in love. Can anyone have much respect for a system of education that insults reason and nature in this way?

Her writings contain many similar opinions, mixed with sentiments that do credit to her head and heart. Yet her religion is so mingled with superstition, and her morality with worldly wisdom, that I would not let a young person read her books unless I could discuss the subjects with them afterwards and point out the contradictions.

Mrs. Chapone’s Letters show such good sense and unaffected humility, and offer so many useful observations, that I mention them only to pay their worthy author this tribute of respect. I cannot, admittedly, always share her opinions; but I always respect her.

The very word respect calls Mrs. Macaulay to mind — without doubt the most able woman this country has ever produced. And yet this woman was allowed to die without her memory receiving the respect it deserved.

Posterity, however, will do her more justice, and will remember that Catharine Macaulay was living proof of intellectual attainments thought to be incompatible with the weakness of her sex. In her style of writing, indeed, no sex is visible; like the sense it expresses, it is strong and clear.

I will not call hers a masculine understanding, because I refuse to allow so arrogant a claim to reason; but I maintain that it was a sound one, and that her judgment, the ripened fruit of deep thought, proved that a woman can acquire judgment in the fullest sense of the word. Having more penetration than shrewdness, and more understanding than imagination, she writes with sober energy and closely reasoned argument; yet sympathy and benevolence lend her sentiments interest, and give her arguments that living warmth which compels the reader to weigh them.*
(*Footnote. Since I share Mrs. Macaulay’s opinions on many branches of education, I refer the reader to her valuable work rather than quote her views in support of mine.)

When I first thought of writing these criticisms, I looked forward to Mrs. Macaulay’s approval with a little of that hopeful eagerness which it has been the business of my life to repress; but I soon learned — with the sick pang of disappointed hope, and the still seriousness of regret — that she was no more!
